We are Blue Atoms, 

We are young programmers from Cape Town, who enjoy coding and solving real world problems, through programming, because we believe if young people face the problems of the world, then they should also be given the opportunity to solve them.
summary:
Atomic Space is an interactive space mission design game in which one to four players design, manage and fly a complete mission, then learn why it succeeded or failed. Players get a mission with a payload, a cost cap and a deadline, then choose the spacecraft, rocket, boosters, instruments, power, radio and orbit. A live review board checks mass, thrust-to-weight, budget, power, data and fuel, so every choice visibly affects the others. Then they fly it: launch, booster separation, operations or a Moon landing, and a scored mission report that explains the result and names the real NASA mission the design resembles.

Real NASA data drives the play. EONET natural events become Earth-mission targets, DONKI solar storms strike the spacecraft and the real Apophis flyby sets a deadline.

We built it in Delphi, the language we learn at school. It comes as a Windows desktop game and as a browser edition, compiled from the same Object Pascal into HTML and JavaScript, so anyone can play from a link. It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into something students can experience.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Atomic Space lets students experience a whole space mission, from concept to operation. Teams of one to four take a mission brief, design the spacecraft and rocket within a budget, pass an engineering review, then fly the mission and get a scored report.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Mission. Each mission has a science goal, a payload, a cost cap and a deadline, and is modelled on a real one: NASA's CAPSTONE CubeSat, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, CLPS/Artemis cargo landers, an Earth-observation satellite, an asteroid flyby and a Europa probe.

2. Design. Players choose the ship, thrusters and number of boosters (desktop edition: 18 designs), and in the browser edition also the orbit, 15 instruments, 12 real launch vehicles and about 40 subsystem options (power, radio, antenna, computer, shielding). Gauges for cost, mass, power, data, science, schedule and success odds update live, and a "ripple" line explains what each change did to everything else.

3. Review board. Red findings block launch (for example a thrust-to-weight ratio below 1.15, or a rocket that cannot lift the mass); amber findings are risks the team chooses to accept.

4. Team go/no-go. Up to four players share four roles (Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Flight and Comms Lead) whose goals pull against each other. Every role must sign off, and any design change resets the sign-offs.

5. Fly. Countdown, lift-off only if thrust beats weight, fuel draining in real time, booster separation at 100,000 ft, then lunar orbit and landing (manual or autopilot) or week-by-week operations with decisions to make.

6. Report. A score out of 100, a grade, the reasons, and the real mission the design resembles. Then improve the design and fly again.

THE SCIENCE

Simplified but real models: Newton's second law and thrust-to-weight for lift-off, the rocket equation for propellant, launch capacity falling as launch energy (C3) rises, solar power falling with the square of distance from the Sun, data rate set by transmitter power and antenna size and falling with the square of distance, and diminishing science returns over time. 765 automated checks compare the engine with real missions (for example, a Juno-sized solar array gives about 500 W at Jupiter).

NASA DATA AT THE CENTRE

Live EONET wildfires, storms and floods decide what the Earth-observation orbit can see; real DONKI solar flares and geomagnetic storms hit the spacecraft on their real dates; NeoWs/JPL data on asteroid Apophis's real 13 April 2029 flyby sets the deadline of the asteroid mission; GIBS Blue Marble imagery is the world map.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students rarely get to try a whole mission. Atomic Space makes the trade-offs concrete: there is never one perfect design, failure is safe, and the game explains why instead of just saying right or wrong. It is free, needs no account, and the browser edition runs on any laptop, tablet or phone, so a class can run a mission in one lesson.

WHY DELPHI, AND TWO EDITIONS

We are learners at the Centre of Science and Technology (COSAT) in Khayelitsha and learn programming in Delphi, so we built Atomic Space in Object Pascal. Delphi gave us a native Windows game that works offline on school computers. A Windows program cannot run from a web link, so we compiled the same Object Pascal to HTML and JavaScript with pas2js and host the browser edition on Vercel.

TOOLS

Delphi 12 Community Edition (VCL) for the desktop edition; pas2js (Free Pascal) for the browser edition; HTML canvas graphics drawn by our own code; Node.js for tests and the NASA data snapshot; Vercel for hosting; GitHub for source code (MIT licence). Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI coding assistant; this is noted in the source files and the README. No AI-generated images, audio or video are used.

LINKS

Play in the browser: https://tradespace-blue-atoms.vercel.app

Windows desktop edition: https://tradespace-blue-atoms.vercel.app/desktop

Presentation: https://tradespace-blue-atoms.vercel.app/presentation

Source code: https://github.com/King-Daniel123/NASA-Space-App-Challenges---BLUE-ATOMS

TEAM BLUE ATOMS (COSAT, Khayelitsha)
